text: Chapter 2 ended with an image sitting in a registry, built and pushed but going nowhere on its own. This lesson is about the thing that actually runs it: a managed cloud container service.

Every one of these services asks for the same two things, starting with the build: a runtime, a build command, a start command, and a port. It's the same information as your Dockerfile's RUN and CMD lines, as form fields instead of file lines.

The second screen is the resource envelope: CPU and memory per instance, environment variables, and the two settings that matter most once real traffic shows up — the autoscaling policy and the health check endpoint the platform pings to decide if an instance is alive.

Once you deploy, the console shows the service moving from pending to running, and you get a real public HTTPS URL plus a service ARN. An app that was a Dockerfile on your laptop an hour ago is now a public endpoint.

This walkthrough used AWS App Runner because it's the most compact version of the flow, but the same two screens exist under different names in Amazon ECS on Fargate, Google Cloud Run, and Azure Container Apps.
A deployed service isn't the same as a service ready for real traffic. Next up: what actually sits in front of that default domain — API gateways and load balancing.
